title: First Index of 1 in a Sorted 0/1 Array
statement:
You are given an array of `n` elements, each either `0` or `1`, sorted in non-decreasing order (so all the zeros come before all the ones). Find the index (0-based) of the **first** `1`. If the array contains no `1`, print `-1`.

**Follow-up:** The interviewer then made the array infinite: it begins with some zeros followed by ones forever, you may read `arr[i]` for any index `i`, but its length is unknown. Find the first `1` in `O(log p)` time, where `p` is the answer, using exponential search: double an index `1, 2, 4, 8, ...` until `arr[index]` is `1`, then binary search inside the last doubled window. An infinite array cannot be supplied through standard input, so the tests here only cover the finite version above.
input_format:
The first line contains an integer `n`.
The second line contains `n` integers, each `0` or `1`, in non-decreasing order.
output_format: Print a single integer: the index of the first `1`, or `-1` if there is none.
constraints: The array is sorted in non-decreasing order

examples.explanation: Indices 0, 1 and 2 hold zeros; index 3 is the first 1.
There is no 1 in the array.
The very first element is already a 1.

hints: Because the array is sorted, once you see a 1 at some index, every later element is also 1.
Binary search for the boundary: if arr[mid] is 1 the answer is at mid or to its left, otherwise it is strictly to the right.
Keep a half-open range [lo, hi) with hi = n. When it collapses, lo == n means there was no 1.
reference:
import sys


def main():
    data = sys.stdin.read().split()
    n = int(data[0])
    a = data[1:1 + n]
    lo, hi = 0, n
    while lo < hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if a[mid] == '1':
            hi = mid
        else:
            lo = mid + 1
    print(lo if lo < n else -1)


main()

import sys

data = sys.stdin.read().split()
n = int(data[0])
a = [int(x) for x in data[1:1 + n]]
ans = -1
for i in range(n):
    if a[i] == 1:
        ans = i
        break
print(ans)
